```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

DietView was written for stomach contents, but what it needs is more general:
a taxon name with a quantity, inside a sampling unit, with covariates. The
same structure describes diet from DNA metabarcoding of scats or gut contents,
pellets and regurgitates, catch composition from a survey haul, or a benthic
grab. This article shows the three pieces that bring such data in:

* `dv_from_wide()` reshapes a wide sample-by-taxon table into the long format;
* `dv_parse_lineage()` splits the lineage strings that pipelines report into
  rank columns;
* `dv_spec(weight_type = )` says what the quantity is, so sequence reads are
  summarized as relative read abundance rather than as a mass.

For prey outside the marine realm, `dv_prepare(taxonomy = "gbif")` resolves
names against the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy with the same rules and the same
review log as WoRMS.

```{r setup}
library(DietView)
```

## 1. A metabarcoding table

A typical output of a metabarcoding pipeline is one row per ASV, a taxonomy
string, and one column of read counts per sample. Here are six ASVs from four
seal scats (made-up numbers):

```{r asv}
asv <- data.frame(
  asv = paste0("ASV", 1:6),
  taxonomy = c(
    "k__Animalia;p__Chordata;c__Actinopteri;o__Gadiformes;f__Gadidae;g__Gadus;s__morhua",
    "k__Animalia;p__Chordata;c__Actinopteri;o__Gadiformes;f__Gadidae;g__Gadus;s__morhua",
    "k__Animalia;p__Chordata;c__Actinopteri;o__Clupeiformes;f__Clupeidae;g__Clupea;s__harengus",
    "k__Animalia;p__Chordata;c__Actinopteri;o__Pleuronectiformes;f__;g__;s__",
    "k__Animalia;p__Mollusca;c__Cephalopoda;o__Myopsida;f__Loliginidae;g__Loligo;s__Loligo sp.",
    "Unassigned"),
  scat1 = c(5200, 800, 0, 300, 0, 40),
  scat2 = c(0, 0, 6100, 0, 900, 0),
  scat3 = c(1500, 0, 1500, 0, 0, 10),
  scat4 = c(0, 0, 0, 2500, 2500, 0))
meta <- data.frame(sample = paste0("scat", 1:4), predator = "grey seal",
                   season = c("winter", "winter", "summer", "summer"))
```

### Reshape and parse

`dv_from_wide()` turns it into one row per ASV in a sample, drops the zeros and
joins the sample metadata. ASV1 and ASV2 carry the same taxonomy;
`collapse_by = "taxonomy"` sums them, so that a taxon counts once per sample in
the shares of records and in %FO:

```{r long}
long <- dv_from_wide(asv, id_cols = c("asv", "taxonomy"), meta = meta,
                     collapse_by = "taxonomy")
long <- dv_parse_lineage(long, "taxonomy")
long[, c("sample", "reads", "order", "genus", "species", "prey_name")]
```

The empty fields (`f__`), the placeholder `Unassigned` and `Loligo sp.` become
`NA`: these records stay in the tree, as the explicit unidentified category
below the deepest rank they reached, exactly as a stomach item identified only
to order.

### Reads are not biomass

Sequence reads measure DNA, not prey mass: digestion, tissue type and primer
bias all distort the link (Deagle et al. 2019). DietView therefore never
labels reads as weight. Two summaries are offered:

* `weight_type = "reads"`: the share of all reads (pooled), which lets the
  samples with most reads dominate;
* `weight_type = "rra"`: the relative read abundance. The reads of each sample
  are divided by its total before summing, so every sample weighs the same and
  the share at a rank is the mean RRA over samples.

The shares of prey records stay available and, with one record per taxon and
sample, are the occurrence-based view; `dv_fo_table()` gives the classical
frequency of occurrence over samples.

```{r prep}
spec <- dv_spec(predator = "predator", stomach = "sample",
                prey_name = "prey_name", weight = "reads",
                weight_type = "rra", covariates = "season")
prep <- dv_prepare(long, spec, taxonomy = "columns", verbose = FALSE)
tree <- dv_tree(prep)
dv_rank_table(tree, "Order")
dv_fo_table(prep, rank = "order")
```

`pct_w` is the mean RRA. Each figure and dashboard labels it as such:

```{r sunburst, eval = FALSE}
dv_sunburst(tree, mode = "weight", title = "Grey seal scats (RRA)")
dv_build_html(prep, output = "seal_scats.html", cross = list("season"))
```

## 2. Which taxonomy?

Three routes, by what the data already carry:

| The data carry | Use | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A lineage string from the assignment step | `dv_parse_lineage()` then `taxonomy = "columns"` | Keeps the reference taxonomy the sequences were assigned with (NCBI, SILVA, BOLD), and needs no network. |
| Prey names, marine prey | `taxonomy = "worms"` | WoRMS is the authority for marine taxa. |
| Prey names, terrestrial or freshwater prey | `taxonomy = "gbif"` | The GBIF Backbone covers all kingdoms. |

The names produced by `dv_parse_lineage()` can also be sent to WoRMS or GBIF,
to harmonize a metabarcoding data set with stomach data classified there:

```{r gbif, eval = FALSE}
prep_gbif <- dv_prepare(long, spec, taxonomy = "gbif", kingdom = "Animalia")
dv_taxonomy_report(prep_gbif)
```

GBIF matches are logged like WoRMS matches, with two extra review flags:
`"higherrank"` (the name is unknown to GBIF, but a coarser taxon in it is
known, so the lineage stops there) and `low_confidence`. The GBIF Backbone has
no class for some groups (ray-finned fishes sit directly under Chordata); the
default `gaps = "label"` fills that rank as `"Chordata (no class)"` rather
than counting the records as unidentified.

## 3. Other compositional data

Catch composition, plankton or benthos tables often come with samples in rows
and taxa in columns. `taxa_in = "columns"` reads that layout:

```{r catch}
haul <- data.frame(haul = c("H1", "H2"), stratum = c("401", "402"),
                   `Gadus morhua` = c(12.4, 0), `Clupea harengus` = c(30.1, 55.0),
                   check.names = FALSE)
catch <- dv_from_wide(haul, taxa_in = "columns", id_cols = c("haul", "stratum"),
                      sample_col = "haul", value_col = "kg")
catch
```

Then declare the haul as the sampling unit, the stratum as the "predator" (or
as a covariate, with a constant predator column), and the weight in kg as a
mass. Everything downstream (sunbursts, covariate strata, the dashboard)
works unchanged.

## 4. What does not fit

Stable isotopes and fatty acids do not identify prey: mixing models
(MixSIAR, simmr, QFASA) estimate the contributions of a few source groups
chosen by the analyst, with posterior uncertainty. A sunburst of posterior
means would hide that uncertainty and the shallow, often functional, grouping
of the sources. DietView is not meant for those outputs; it can, however, hold
the stomach or DNA data from the same predators on one taxonomic backbone, the
reference against which isotope-based diets are often compared.

## References

Deagle, B. E., Thomas, A. C., McInnes, J. C., Clarke, L. J., Vesterinen,
E. J., Clare, E. L., Kartzinel, T. R., & Eveson, J. P. (2019). Counting with
DNA in metabarcoding studies: How should we convert sequence reads to dietary
data? *Molecular Ecology*, 28(2), 391-406.
